name: Colin Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I cycle to the jobcentre on Tanner Road for my fortnightly sign-on, or I'm at the kitchen table in my flat on Fenwick Court sending applications. Afternoons I do a free logistics-software course online, then I walk about to clear my head. Until March I was a shift lead at the Brandt distribution centre out by the ring road, running a team of twelve pickers. They brought in automated sorting lines and cut two of the three shifts. I was also the union rep for my shift, so that didn't help my case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype would be fine by me, but I've already watched the machines come into my warehouse, so I'm a bit sceptical of the word hype. Still, I'd take a slow version over a fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same story as always: a few tasks get automated and the company counts the savings. At the pub I'd say the sorting lines at the Brandt distribution centre didn't need any AI hype to cost me my job. They just needed a manager with a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think the plateau means warehouse and logistics jobs keep slowly thinning out, but not overnight. That gives me time to find a supervisor role at one of the older sites that hasn't automated yet. I'm still the guy who lost his job, and that sits in the back of my mind at every interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the logistics-software course in about eight weeks and renew my forklift ticket, which runs out in January. I'd apply to roughly ten places a week, including the council depots and the hospital supplies unit. I'd also use a chatbot to tidy my CV, because my spelling isn't great, but I'd check every line myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, not scared. I'm used to scraping by, and the rent on Fenwick Court is due on the first no matter what. It's a steady grind rather than a drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a warehouse supervisor job at an older site actually come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone retiring or a site getting more orders, so it's partly luck and who you know. I'd ring my old colleagues, like Dev, who now works at a pallet firm in Ashby. People hire people they trust, and I'd lean on that more than on any online form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check every line of the chatbot's CV. What are you checking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For things I'd never say. It once wrote that I 'spearheaded cross-functional synergy', which is nonsense. I want it to sound like a shift lead who got twelve people through a Christmas rush, because that's the truth and the people reading it know the difference.

say: I'd say automation costs jobs once a manager with a **spreadsheet** decides it should.
I'd say the sorting lines didn't need **AI hype** to end my shift.
think: Warehouse jobs keep **thinning slowly**, which leaves time to find an older site.
I'm the one who **lost his job**, and that sits behind every interview.
do: Finish the logistics-software course in about **eight weeks**.
Apply to ten places a week, including the **hospital supplies** unit.
feel: Flat rather than scared, because the **rent** is due on the first regardless.
S0.quote: The sorting lines at the Brandt distribution centre didn't need any AI hype to cost me my job. They just needed a manager with a spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Uses a chatbot for **spelling** but checks every line, a cautious style of adopting tools.
Relies on a **network** of old colleagues more than online forms.
Mood is anxious from the current job loss and no savings, not from AI hype.

steps.text: Finish the logistics-software course online over the next eight weeks
Renew the forklift ticket before it runs out in January
Use a chatbot to tidy the CV and then check each line
Apply to ten warehouse and supplies jobs a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one is closer to what I saw. Planning, booking and ordering are exactly what the new software at Brandt does now. The hands-on bits are still done by people for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs a plan, not a shrug. Retraining should be paid for, and the company that automates should help the workers it lets go. I'd bring it up at the union branch, since I'm still a member even though I'm out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my old job, the one organising a team and planning shifts, is mostly thinking work now, and that's what the software takes first. The picking and loading stays human a bit longer, which is why I'd go back to the floor if I had to. I'm not too proud for it, but the pay is lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the software course, then aim for a role where I work with the systems rather than get replaced by them, like a stock controller or a systems clerk. I'd also keep my forklift and a health-and-safety ticket current. And I'd start using the chatbot a few times a week to learn what the planning tools do, so I'm not a stranger to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but busy. When I'm busy the worry's quieter, but it always shows up after nine at night when the course is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would going back to the floor actually mean for your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three or four pounds an hour less than I was on, and no supervisor allowance. On benefits that still looks better than what I get now, but I'd be anxious about my place in a queue of younger blokes. I'd take a floor job again, because rent doesn't wait for pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the chatbot a few times a week. What would you ask it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How stock control software works, what a warehouse management system does, and which questions interviewers might ask me. I'd also ask it to explain a contract in plain words. It's like a patient colleague who doesn't mind me asking twice.

say: I'd say retraining should be **paid for** by companies that automate.
I'd raise it at the **union branch**, where I'm still a member.
think: Planning shifts is **thinking work**, so the software takes that first.
Picking and loading stay human longer, so I'd **go back** to the floor for lower pay.
do: Finish the software course and aim for a **stock controller** role.
Keep the forklift and **health-and-safety** tickets current.
Use a chatbot a few times a week to learn the **planning tools**.
feel: Uneasy but busy, and the worry returns **after nine** at night.
S1.quote: I'd take a floor job again, because rent doesn't wait for pride.
fieldNote: Understands his own job as **thinking work** at risk, and the floor as a fallback.
Treats the chatbot like a **patient colleague** for learning.
Pride is explicitly set aside because of the rent.

steps.text: Apply for stock controller and systems clerk jobs at local firms
Ask a chatbot to explain warehouse management systems each week
Finish the logistics-software course and get the certificate
Raise paid retraining at the union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's roughly the length of the lease on my flat, which is a strange comparison to make, but it's where my head went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now: income support, a shorter week, and a tax on firms that replace thousands of people with machines. I'd go to the demo outside the town hall and I'd sign anything the union put in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think that in two years nearly all the desk and planning work goes, and the floor goes a few years after. I'd be competing with people from offices who'd drop down to warehouse jobs. I'm thirty-four with no savings, and I don't see a soft landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union and to the council advice centre in the first month to find out what support already exists. I'd cut my phone and streaming, move to a cheaper flat share if I can find one, and stack any cash into a rent buffer. And I'd still finish the software course, because it's cheap and it keeps me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stomach drops when I imagine it. It's like being on a forklift with the brakes gone, and nobody's shouting, because nobody's looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you moved into a flat share, what would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privacy and probably a longer bus ride to the jobcentre. But it'd cut rent by about a third, which in my budget is the difference between eating properly and not. I did a share when I was twenty-two, so I know I can do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots do hands-on work help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, in the sense that the floor jobs hold on until 2031. But there'd be queues round the block for them, as desk workers pile in, so the gap isn't really mine. It's more like a delay on the pay cut.

say: I'd say governments need **income support** and a tax on firms that replace thousands.
I'd join the demo at the **town hall** and sign the union's petitions.
think: In two years desk and planning work goes, and office workers **drop down** into warehouse jobs.
I have **no savings** and don't see a soft landing.
do: Visit the union and the council **advice centre** in the first month.
Cut phone and streaming, and move to a **flat share** to save about a third.
Still finish the **software course** because it's cheap and keeps me moving.
feel: My stomach drops, like a forklift with the **brakes gone** and nobody looking.
S2.quote: I'm thirty-four with no savings, and I don't see a soft landing.
fieldNote: Expects **competition from office workers** for floor jobs, a sharp read of the scenario.
Practical first moves: advice centre, flat share, keep the course going.
Hands-on delay of three years is seen as a **delayed pay cut**, not relief.

steps.text: Visit the council advice centre and the union in the first month
Cancel streaming and cut the phone plan to the cheapest one
Move into a flat share to cut rent by about a third
Go to the town hall demo and sign the union petition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of runway. It's still quick, but it's not quite the cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that if five years is what we've got, we should spend it building the safety net, not arguing about whether it's real. I'd tell the lads from the Brandt warehouse to join the union branch now, because a lonely worker has no clout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I can make myself useful to the new systems in five years, maybe working in a team that looks after automated lines. It's not guaranteed, but I'd bet on being the guy who knows the floor and the screen. Warehouse robots can't spot a mislabelled pallet the way a human eye can, at least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the logistics course, then take a night class in basic programming and automation. I'd apply for a technician trainee spot at a firm that runs automated lines. I'd also push to get a union learning rep role so I can help other out-of-work members book courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. I'd still be worried about money in the meantime, but the horizon looks like it's got a path on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between the two-year picture and this five-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I can take the technician route and have something on my CV. I'd also still be around when the hands-on jobs start to change, which gives me a chance to move before the crush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the technician plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms hiring technicians might want a degree or a few years' experience I don't have, or they'd just take a younger person. The other risk is that my benefits get cut during the course. I'd have to ask the jobcentre whether a trainee spot counts as work-ready, and I don't trust the answer to be consistent.

say: I'd say we should spend five years building the **safety net**, not arguing if it's real.
I'd tell the Brandt lads to join the **union branch** now.
think: In five years I could work on a team that **looks after** automated lines.
I'm the guy who knows both the **floor and the screen**.
do: Finish the logistics course, then a night class in **basic automation**.
Apply for a **technician trainee** spot at a firm with automated lines.
Take a union **learning rep** role to help others book courses.
feel: Steadier, because the horizon has a **path** on it, though money is tight until then.
S3.quote: I'd tell the lads from the Brandt warehouse to join the union branch now, because a lonely worker has no clout.
fieldNote: Sees a niche in being the person who knows **floor and screen** both.
Doubts the jobcentre will treat a **trainee spot** consistently.
Collective action is a practical tool for him, not just a slogan.

steps.text: Finish the logistics course, then take a night class in basic automation
Apply for technician trainee jobs at firms with automated lines
Become a union learning rep and help others book courses
Ask a chatbot to explain how automated sorting lines are maintained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to do a degree or an apprenticeship. I'll be forty-four, and that's still a working life ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly: retraining paid by the companies that benefit, reduced hours and decent pensions. I'd talk about it at the branch and push our MP to take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think ten years lets me work and learn at once. I could take an apprenticeship in automation maintenance and be a technician by thirty-eight. I still feel angry about Brandt, because the lines that replaced us were paid out of our shift cuts, but I'd rather turn the anger into a skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the technician pathway through a college and a firm that sponsors apprentices. I'd save a little every month once I'm in paid training, and slowly build a rent buffer. I'd also keep my union membership and volunteer on the learning rep side, since it's good company and it keeps me in the loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but impatient. Ten years should feel safe, but my bank balance today is zero, so it doesn't feel safe yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister Joan about ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to stop fretting about her kids' future and to push them into practical, hands-on things alongside the screens. I'd tell her I'd be a technician by then and we'd laugh about the old days. And I'd tell her not to loan me money, because I'd rather earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the benefits and the training funds are still there when I need them. Governments change, and a scheme can vanish in one budget. I'd want a promise written into law and not a ministerial speech.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this **properly**, with retraining paid by the winners.
I'd push our **MP** to take reduced hours and pensions seriously.
think: I could take an **apprenticeship** in automation maintenance and be a technician by thirty-eight.
I'd rather turn my **anger** about Brandt into a skill.
do: Start a technician **apprenticeship** through a college and a sponsoring firm.
Build a small **rent buffer** once I'm in paid training.
Volunteer as a union **learning rep** to stay in the loop.
feel: Hopeful but **impatient**, because my bank balance is zero today.
S4.quote: Governments change, and a scheme can vanish in one budget. I'd want a promise written into law and not a ministerial speech.
fieldNote: Turns **anger at Brandt** into a skill plan.
Wants guarantees in **law**, a progressive reflex.
Mood stays anxious because the bank balance is zero today.

steps.text: Start an automation maintenance apprenticeship with a sponsoring firm
Save a little every month once in paid training
Volunteer as union learning rep for other out-of-work members
Write to our MP asking for retraining funds set in law

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Two years is enough time for the desk work to vanish before I've gotten anywhere with the course, and with no savings I can't absorb a hit. What would help is paid retraining that's guaranteed in law, support for rent while I'm studying, and companies that automate being asked to chip in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how little the jobcentre knows about warehouse work. They keep sending me to cleaning jobs and call centres. And I'd say don't treat us ex-shift-leads as a statistic, because we're the ones who can actually show a robot where the pallets go.

headlineQuote: Don't treat us ex-shift-leads as a statistic, because we're the ones who can actually show a robot where the pallets go.
portrait: Colin is **34**, lives alone on Fenwick Court, and has been out of work since **March** after Brandt automated its sorting lines.
He was a shift lead of twelve pickers and a union rep, and now sends about ten applications a week.
He takes AI up **slowly and carefully**, as a spelling helper and a patient teacher.
He blames managers with spreadsheets, wants **law-backed** retraining, and is anxious in every scenario because his cushion is zero.
He plans to become a technician who knows the **floor and the screen**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** guaranteed in law, with rent support while he studies.
Companies that automate should **chip in** for the workers they let go.
